profile.name: Furong Jia
profile.description: Furong Jia is a Computer Science Ph.D. student at Duke University studying how data shapes LLM behavior and how LLMs interpret data, with interests in probabilistic knowledge, AI agents, and AI for healthcare.

about: Hi! I am a third-year Computer Science PhD student at Duke University, supervised by Prof. Monica Agrawal. Previously, I received a B.S. in Computer Science and a B.S. in Applied and Computational Mathematics from University of Southern California, where I was fortunate to work with Prof. Yan Liu, Prof. Jesse Thomason, and Prof. Maja Matarić.

Research: I study how data shapes LLM behavior and how LLMs interpret data, with the broader goal of understanding what makes these systems reliable, interpretable, and robust. My work examines how pretraining data and inference-time inputs influence model reasoning, including how faithfully LLMs acquire probabilistic knowledge from text. My research also spans diverse data (text, time series, and multimodal inputs), including developing forecasting methods and studying model behavior under distribution shift. Building on this, I now study LLM agents for healthcare and scientific discovery: when agent design actually matters, and how agents can analyze and explain clinical data.
Feel free to reach out to me if you'd like to discuss research or explore potential collaboration!

projects.title: Harnesses for LLM-driven discovery
bullets: To separate a harness's effect from task, model, and budget, we led a controlled comparison of 11 search harnesses on mathematical construction, GPU kernel optimization, and language-model training. Harness choice often mattered more than a model upgrade, but the winner depended on the setup: counting budget in candidates instead of API cost changed the top harness in half of the settings, switching the model reversed 41% of harness pairs, and running the autoresearch loop via a coding agent, not a fixed pipeline, benefited from using the stronger model but rarely the weaker.

projects.title: Probabilistic knowledge from pretraining
bullets: We studied how faithfully LLMs acquire probabilistic knowledge from pretraining text. We built a controlled continual-pretraining framework where known data-generating networks define ground-truth distributions, synthetic clinical-style corpora verbalize sampled configurations, and OLMo-2 models are evaluated by comparing native next-token probabilities with ground-truth posteriors. We found that models recover individual probabilities well but compress the relations between them, understating how far apart outcomes are and how much evidence should move a prediction. We call this relational compression, which is typically under-measured by standard metrics because they score each probability in isolation.

projects.title: Interpreting dataset shift in clinical notes
bullets: We addressed the need to explain, more than just detect, distribution shifts in clinical text. We established an extensible benchmark suite that induces synthetic shifts using real clinical notes, developed methods for evaluating generated shift explanations, and introduced SIReNs, an end-to-end approach that explains distributional differences by selecting representative notes from each distribution. We are also extending this work to benchmark agent capabilities and agent harnesses for interpreting shifts in multi-factorial settings and more general textual domains.

projects.title: Where LLMs learn clinical knowledge
bullets: We examined how evidence in pretraining corpora shapes clinical LLM behavior. We linked keyword-pair occurrences in pretraining data to model performance on clinical jargon understanding and unsupported medical claims, curated MedLingo from real-world clinical-note abbreviations, and analyzed sources of clinical information in pretraining datasets to guide future corpus design.

projects.title: Counting baselines for diagnosis
bullets: We tested how much of LLMs' diagnostic accuracy can be explained by pretraining-corpus statistics. We built FBPR, a Naive Bayes ranker that scores MedQA diagnoses using concept–diagnosis co-occurrence counts from an LLM's pretraining corpus (or its open reproduction), and found that it matches that LLM's diagnostic accuracy. The two get largely different questions right, and a simple hybrid of the two beats both.

projects.title: Large Language Models for Multimodal Time Series Forecasting
bullets: We introduced GPT4MTS, a prompt-based framework that fuses numeric time series with text. We also built a GDELT-derived multimodal news impact dataset and showed consistent forecasting gains over strong unimodal baselines, demonstrating effective multimodal fusion and the value of extra-textual information.

We developed TEMPO, a GPT architecture-based time series framework that combines seasonal trend decomposition with adaptive, selection-based prompting for non-stationary distribution shift. It achieves zero-shot state-of-the-art across diverse and unseen (including multi-modal) benchmarks, indicating strong potential as a foundation model for time series forecasting.

projects.title: Parameter-efficient finetuning for Multimodal Continual Learning
bullets: We applied parameter-efficient knowledge transfer using adapters in multimodal models for visual question answering tasks. We implemented and trained model architectures on multiple vision-language tasks (VQAv2, Visual7W, VQA-Abstract, VizWiz, DAQUAR) to enhance forward transfer and reduce knowledge forgetting.
